source_text: ὥσπερ προθυμίαις εἰς τοῦτο διᾴττουσιν, καὶ σφριγώσῃ διανοίᾳ, καὶ νῷ διεγηγερμένῳ, καὶ ἀκμαιοτάταις ὁρμαῖς ἴενται πρὸς κατόρθωσιν, ὧν ἂν δεήσῃ πληροῦν, καὶ ἀποπεραίνειν δύνασθαι τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν. Εἶεν δ' ἂν οὗτοι, κατά γε τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἱστορίας ὑποδηλούμενον οἱ ἀπὸ εἰκοσαετοῦς καὶ ἕως ἑξήκοντα ἔτους· ἀνέρχεται μὲν γὰρ ἕως ἑξηκοστοῦ λοιπὸν ἔτους, εὐσθενὲς εἶναι τὸ σῶμα, καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀκμαιοτάτοις κινήμασι. Βέβηκε δὲ ἤδη καὶ ἔῤῥωταί πως ὁ νοῦς, καὶ μάλα ἐπιτηδείως ἔχει πρὸς παραδοχὴν, ὧν ἂν ἕλοιτο μαθεῖν. Ὁ δὲ εἰδὼς τὸ πλάσμα ἡμῶν, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, ἔγνω που πάντως τοιάνδε τινὰ καὶ ἐν ψυχαῖς ἡλικίαν. Ἐξ ὁμοιώσεων γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῶν σωματικῶν διέρπει που πάντως ἐπὶ τὰ νοητά. Εἴτ' οὖν ἄρσεν εἴη τυχὸν, εἴτ' οὖν θήλεια, τῆς νοητῆς ἡλικίας ἐν ἀκμαῖς ἔτι κείμενοι, προσκομιζόντων τὰ ὡρισμένα, τουτέστιν, ἄρσην, ὡς ἐν διδράχμοις πεντήκοντα τὸν ἀρτίως ἔχοντα, καὶ ὅτι μάλιστα τελεώτατον, τῆς πνευματικῆς λατρείας καρπὸν, ὃς διὰ τῶν ἑπτάκις ἑπτὰ, πρὸς λῆξιν ἤδη τὴν ἀνωτάτω, καὶ εἰς τελειότητα μεμαρτυρημένος ὁρᾶται σαφῶς. Ἡ δέ γε θήλεια πάλιν, ὡς ἐν διδράχμοις τριάκοντα· μεῖον μὲν γὰρ ἢ τὸ ἄρσεν εὐδοκιμεῖ, προσκομίζει δὴ οὖν ὅμως ὡς κατ' ἰδίαν φύσιν, τὸν ἐν τελειότητι καὶ πόνῳ καρπὸν, ὡς διὰ τριῶν δεκάδων ὑποδηλούμενον. Ὁ δὲ ἀπὸ πενταετοῦς, καὶ ἕως εἰκοσαετοῦς, εἰ μὲν ἄρσεν εἴη, διδράχμων εἴκοσι ποιεῖται κατάθεσιν. Εἰ δέ γε θήλεια, δέκα. Ἐκ πέντε γὰρ, οἶμαι, καὶ μόλις ἐτῶν, ἄρχεταί πως ὁ νοῦς ἀναμύειν ὥσπερ εἰς σύνεσιν, νηπιοπρεπῆ μὲν ἔτι καὶ ἀσθενῆ, πλὴν ἰοῦσαν ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ ἄμεινον, ἐπίδοσιν δὲ τὴν εἰς τὸ ἀείπως εὐσθενὲς τὸ σῶμα ποιεῖται Ἢ οὐ συνιεῖς ὃ λέγω; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Καὶ μάλα. {ΚΥΡ.} Συμμεμέτρηται μὲν οὖν ταῖς πνευματικαῖς εὐρωστίαις καὶ ὁ παρ' ἑκάστου καρπός. Κατόπιν δὲ πανταχοῦ τὸ θῆλυ τοῦ ἄρσενος, καὶ ἐν ἡμίσει πολλάκις. Ὅτι γὰρ τὸ σκεῦος ἀσθενὲς, μεμαρτύρηκε σαφῶς ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος. Λείπεται δὲ τῆς ἀνδρῶν εὐφυΐας, καὶ σιωπᾷ μὲν ἐν ἐκκλησίαις. Οὐ γὰρ πεπίστευται λόγον, εὐσθενὲς δὲ οὔτι που πρὸς κατόρθωσιν ἀρετῆς, ὡς ἂν ὁρῷτο ἄρσεν. Ἀπὸ δέ γε μηνιαίου, φησὶ, καὶ ἕως πενταετοῦς, πέντε μὲν δίδραχμα τὸ ἄρσεν· τρία δὲ αὖ, τὸ θῆλυ. Καί τοι τίς γένοιτο παρὰ βρεφῶν ὁ καρπός; Οὐκοῦν πως ἀρτιγενὲς ἐν Χριστῷ παιδίον ὁ λόγος ἡμῖν ὑπαινίττεται, οἷς καὶ τὸ γάλα πρέπειν εἰς τροφὴν ὁ ἱερὸς ἔφη Παῦλος. Τῶν γὰρ ἄρτι κεκλημένων διὰ τῆς πίστεως, καὶ νηπιαζόντων ἔτι, βραχὺς ὁ καρπός· καὶ τοῦτο εἰδότες οἱ θεσπέσιοι μαθηταὶ, τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν ἐπιστέλλουσι, καὶ τῆς πλείστης ὅσης εὐαγγελικῆς ἐντολῆς δοθείσης παρὰ Χριστοῦ, φυλάττεσθαι δεῖν ἀπό τε πορνείας καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ αἵματος. Ταῦτα δὲ δρῶντας εὐπράξειν ἔφασκον. Οὐ γάρ τοι τοῖς ἄγαν φορτικοῖς καταβαρύνεσθαι χρὴ τὸν τρυφερὸν ἔτι καὶ νηπιάζοντα νοῦν. Προσετίθη δὲ ὁ νόμος, ἐξαιτεῖσθαι δεῖν τοὺς ἀπὸ ἑξακονταετοῦς καὶ ἐπάνω, ἄρσενα μὲν, δέκα καὶ πέντε δίδραχμα, θήλειαν δὲ, δέκα. Τὸ γὰρ ἤδη νενευ
pass_a_gloss: Cyril (continuing): ...with eagernesses (προθυμίαις) as it were dart (διᾴττουσιν) toward this, and with a swelling/vigorous (σφριγώσῃ) understanding (διανοίᾳ) and an awakened (διεγηγερμένῳ) mind (νῷ) and most vigorous (ἀκμαιοτάταις) impulses (ὁρμαῖς) go toward accomplishment (κατόρθωσις) of whatever must be fulfilled, and to be able to complete what seems good to him (τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν). These would be, according to what is suggested (ὑποδηλούμενον) by the history, those from twenty years to sixty [Lev 27:3]; for it extends (ἀνέρχεται) up to the sixtieth year that the body is strong (εὐσθενές) and in its most vigorous movements (κινήμασι). The mind (νοῦς) has already become steady (βέβηκε) and somewhat strong (ἔρρωται), and is very fit (ἐπιτηδείως) for receiving (παραδοχή) what it might choose to learn. He who knows our formation (πλάσμα), as written [Ps 102:14 LXX], surely knew such an age (ἡλικία) also in souls (ψυχαῖς). For from likenesses (ὁμοιώσεων) of bodily things the account creeps through (διέρπει) to the intelligible (νοητά). Whether male (ἄρσεν) or female (θήλεια), lying still in the peaks (ἀκμαῖς) of the intelligible age, let them bring the fixed things (ὡρισμένα): that is, the male, as in fifty didrachms (διδράχμοις), the fruit (καρπός) of spiritual worship (λατρεία) in perfect condition (ἀρτίως ἔχοντα) and most perfect (τελεώτατον), which through the seven times seven is clearly seen attested (μεμαρτυρημένος) toward the highest end (λῆξις) and unto perfection (τελειότης). The female again as in thirty didrachms; for she is esteemed (εὐδοκιμεῖ) less than the male, yet brings according to her own nature (φύσιν) the fruit in perfection and labor (πόνῳ), as suggested through three decades (δεκάδων). The one from five to twenty years, if male, makes a deposit (κατάθεσις) of twenty didrachms; if female, ten [Lev 27:5]. For from five years, I think, and barely (μόλις), the mind begins to open its eyes (ἀναμύειν) as it were to understanding (σύνεσις), still childlike (νηπιοπρεπῆ) and weak, yet going toward the better; and the body makes progress (ἐπίδοσις) toward ever (ἀείπως) strong. Or do you not understand what I say? Palladius: Very much. Cyril: The fruit from each has been measured together with (συμμεμέτρηται) spiritual strengths (εὐρωστίαις). Everywhere the female behind (κατόπιν) the male, and often at half (ἡμίσει). For that the vessel (σκεῦος) is weak the inspired Paul clearly witnessed [1 Pet 3:7]. She falls short (λείπεται) of the natural gift (εὐφυΐα) of men and keeps silent (σιωπᾷ) in churches [1 Cor 14:34]. For she has not been entrusted (πεπίστευται) with the word (λόγον), and is not at all strong for the accomplishment of virtue (ἀρετή) as the male would be seen. From a month old, he says, to five years, the male five didrachms, the female three [Lev 27:6]. Yet what fruit could come from infants (βρεφῶν)? So the account hints (ὑπαινίττεται) at the newborn (ἀρτιγενές) child in Christ, for whom the holy Paul said milk (γάλα) is fitting for food [1 Cor 3:1-2]. For of those just called through faith and still being infants (νηπιαζόντων) the fruit is short (βραχύς). Knowing this the inspired disciples, writing to those from the nations (ἐθνῶν), though very much gospel commandment (εὐαγγελικῆς ἐντολῆς) had been given by Christ, [said they] must guard themselves from fornication (πορνεία), what is strangled (πνικτόν) and blood (αἷμα); doing these things, they said, they would do well (εὐπράξειν) [Acts 15:28-29]. For the still tender (τρυφερόν) and infant mind must not be weighed down (καταβαρύνεσθαι) with very heavy things (φορτικοῖς). The law added that from those sixty years and over must be required, male fifteen didrachms, female ten [Lev 27:7]. For what has already sunk (νενευκός) into the feeble (ἄναλκι) and powerless (ἀδρανές)...
pass_b_english: Cyril: …zeal, as it were, rush toward it, and with a vigorous understanding, a wakeful mind and the strongest drive, they press on to accomplish whatever must be fulfilled, and to be able to carry out what is pleasing to him. According to what the history suggests, these would be the people from twenty years old up to sixty (Leviticus 27:3). For up to the sixtieth year the body stays strong and at its most vigorous in its movements. By then the mind, too, is settled and in a way strong, and it is very well suited to take in whatever it chooses to learn. And he who knows our frame, as it is written (Psalm 103:14), surely knew that there is such an age in souls also. For the passage, no doubt, moves, by likenesses drawn from bodily things, to the things perceived by the mind. So, whether one is male or female, let those who are still in the prime of that inward age bring what has been appointed. That is, let the male bring, in the form, as it were, of fifty didrachms, the fruit of spiritual worship, sound and as perfect as can be; for by way of seven times seven it is plainly seen to reach the highest goal and to be attested as perfect. The female, again, brings it in the form, as it were, of thirty didrachms (Leviticus 27:4). For she is held in less esteem than the male, yet she still brings, in keeping with her own nature, a fruit marked by perfection and toil, as the three tens suggest. The one from five years old up to twenty, if male, pays twenty didrachms; if female, ten (Leviticus 27:5). For from the age of five, I think, and barely then, the mind begins in a way to open its eyes, as it were, to understanding. That understanding is still childish and weak, but it is moving toward the better, and the body is growing ever stronger. Or do you not understand what I mean?

Cyril: So the fruit from each person is measured in proportion to spiritual strength. Everywhere the female comes after the male, and often at half. For the inspired Paul has plainly testified that the vessel is weak (1 Peter 3:7). She falls short of the natural ability of men, and she keeps silent in the churches (1 Corinthians 14:34). For she has not been entrusted with the word, and she is by no means as strong for achieving virtue as the male is seen to be. From one month old, it says, up to five years, the male gives five didrachms, and the female, for her part, three (Leviticus 27:6). And yet what fruit could come from infants? So in a way the passage hints to us at the newborn child in Christ, those for whom, as the holy Paul said, milk is the fitting food (1 Corinthians 3:1–2). For the fruit of those who have only just been called through faith and are still infants is small. Knowing this, the inspired disciples, writing to those from the Gentiles, even though Christ had given a very great body of Gospel commandments, told them that they must keep themselves from fornication, from what is strangled and from blood; and they said that those who did these things would do well (Acts 15:28–29). For a mind that is still tender and childish must not be weighed down with very heavy burdens. The law added that from those sixty years old and over, fifteen didrachms must be required for a male and ten for a female (Leviticus 27:7). For what has already declined into feebleness and weakness…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 16. Translated afresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withdrawn English was not used for wording.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; a column may cut mid-sentence or mid-word.

PG 68.1037. Opens mid-sentence (‘with warmer zeal…’) from §14. τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν is printed unaspirated; taken as ‘what is pleasing to him’ (God); αὑτῷ, ‘what seems good to himself’, is possible but less likely in context. ‘He who knows our frame’: LXX Psalm 102:14 (ἔγνω τὸ πλάσμα ἡμῶν) = English Psalm 103:14. ‘Seven times seven’: Cyril reads fifty as the completion that follows forty-nine. ‘The vessel is weak’ (τὸ σκεῦος ἀσθενές) is the wording of 1 Peter 3:7 (ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει), which Cyril here attributes to Paul; the attribution is kept as he wrote it and the citation gives the actual verse. ‘She has not been entrusted with the word’ may echo 1 Timothy 2:12; left uncited. ‘Newborn child’ (ἀρτιγενές) may also echo 1 Peter 2:2; Cyril names Paul, so 1 Corinthians 3:1–2 is cited (compare Hebrews 5:12–13). The apostolic decree (fornication, what is strangled, blood; ‘you will do well’) is Acts 15:28–29 (also 15:20); ‘not be weighed down with heavy burdens’ echoes 15:28 and is covered by that citation. Cyril’s view of women is translated as he states it, without softening. Section ends mid-sentence, continued in §16. νοητῆς ἡλικίας is the ‘inward’ (mental) age, not πνευματικός; rendered ‘that inward age’. νηπιοπρεπῆ … ἰοῦσαν agree with σύνεσιν, so ‘childish and weak’ describes the understanding.
